title: Later Columbia records and D.H. Holmes patronage
summary: Foster says later records were made after the band broke up, and that the D.H. Holmes family supplied instruments free because they liked the band.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well see we always practiced bass, bass violin, drum and banjo. Worked the same thing. Stoked the very same thing. Same thing. Practice. That's a resident. A bit of a resident. I see those other records we record that after we broke the band up.
I saw a stand. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand.
Yeah. I saw a stand. Yeah. I saw a stand. Yeah.

Yeah. Our band. Oh yeah, we had some records. Well they used to follow us all the time, you know. And anything that we wanted in the line instrument, we didn't have to pay for it, they'd give it to us.
And that was the man of the D.H. Holmes?
One of the sons, the president's son.
Well they used to like our band, you know. At that time.
I don't have any of those Columbia records here, the later ones.

And you see, well, we had a lot of friends, you know what I mean? Yeah. Well they used to, anything that we said we wanted, well they had to fix that, and all we had to do is just go to the store and tell them the charges to Mr. So-and-so. No kidding. Well it was all them boys, you know, they just were having fun. They wasn't playing for no living, they just were having fun like that, you see. Now he gave me a symbol there, it cost $65 at that time. See, well I imagine right now, I imagine right now, that symbol that he gave me was somewhere around about $150 or $165.
